guide.title: Dysrhythmia Recognition
guide.lead: Read the strip the same way every time, then look at the patient. The rhythm name matters less than one question: is this patient stable? Unstable slow means atropine and pacing. Unstable fast means electricity.

steps.title: Rhythm
steps.text: Regular, regularly irregular, or irregularly irregular.

steps.title: PR interval
steps.text: Normal 0.12–0.20 s. Longer: AV block. Changing: Wenckebach.

steps.title: QRS width
steps.text: Narrow less than 0.12 s (from above the ventricles); wide 0.12 s or more.

steps.title: Now the patient
steps.text: Unstable = low BP, altered mental status, shock signs, ischemic chest pain or acute heart failure.

sections.title: With a pulse and unstable

steps.text: Oxygen if hypoxic; 12-lead; look for a cause (MI, drugs, high potassium).
Atropine 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes, maximum 3 mg.
Or infusion: dopamine 5–20 mcg/kg/min or epinephrine 2–10 mcg/min.
Stable narrow regular (SVT): vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva) first.
Then adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push with a flush, then 12 mg.
Stable wide regular: treat as VT; amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes or expert advice.

sections.after: Atropine often fails in Mobitz II and complete heart block with a wide QRS: go to pacing.

sections.title: Heart blocks at a glance
rows: PR longer than 0.20 s, every P conducted
PR lengthens until a QRS drops
High: may progress; prepare to pace

quiz.q: Regular rhythm at 48/min, normal P waves, PR 0.16 s, narrow QRS. Dizzy, BP 82/50. Rhythm and first drug?
options: Symptomatic sinus bradycardia: atropine 1 mg IV, pace if no response
quiz.explanation: Repeat every 3–5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg.

quiz.q: A "sawtooth" baseline in II, III and aVF is:
quiz.explanation: AF has a chaotic baseline with no clear waves.

quiz.q: Unresponsive, BP 70/40. P waves at 90/min and wide QRS at 38/min with no relationship. Rhythm and priority?
options: Complete heart block with a ventricular escape: pace and transport
quiz.explanation: Atropine rarely works with a wide-QRS escape.

quiz.q: PR lengthens beat by beat until a QRS drops. This is:
quiz.explanation: Usually at the AV node and lower risk.
Check the pulse deficit and rate.

quiz.q: First step for a stable patient in SVT:
options: Vagal manoeuvres such as the modified Valsalva

quiz.q: Fast rhythm with chest pain, BP 70/40 and confusion. Treatment?
Maximum total atropine dose for bradycardia:

quiz.explanation: A wide fast rhythm is VT until proven otherwise.

quiz.q: Organised electrical activity on the monitor, but no pulse:
options: PEA: CPR, epinephrine, look for the cause

flashcards.question: Strip reading in order
flashcards.answer: Rate, rhythm, P waves, PR interval, QRS width. Then: is the patient stable?

flashcards.question: Sinus tachycardia vs sinus bradycardia
flashcards.answer: Above 100/min vs below 60/min. Both have normal P waves before every QRS.

flashcards.question: AF vs atrial flutter
flashcards.answer: AF: no P waves, irregularly irregular. Flutter: sawtooth waves (II, III, aVF), often regular.

flashcards.question: Wide, regular, fast, no P waves
flashcards.answer: Ventricular tachycardia. No pulse: defibrillate. Pulse and unstable: synchronized cardioversion. Stable: amiodarone or expert advice.

flashcards.question: Shockable arrest rhythms
flashcards.answer: VF and pulseless VT. Asystole and PEA are not shockable.

flashcards.question: PEA
flashcards.answer: Organised electrical activity without a pulse. CPR, epinephrine, and find the reversible cause (Hs and Ts).

flashcards.question: Mobitz I vs Mobitz II
flashcards.answer: I: PR lengthens until a QRS drops (usually benign). II: fixed PR with sudden drops (dangerous, prepare to pace).

flashcards.question: Third-degree (complete) block
flashcards.answer: P waves and QRS complexes unrelated, each at its own rate. Pace.

critical.scenario: An 82-year-old on metoprolol is pale, sweaty and confused. BP 78/44, HR 38. Regular rhythm with normal P waves, normal PR and narrow QRS.
critical.question: Rhythm and immediate treatment?

options.t: Symptomatic sinus bradycardia: atropine 1 mg IV, pacing if no response
options.f: Correct. Think of the beta-blocker too.
There are normal P waves; amiodarone slows the heart further.

critical.explanation: Atropine 1 mg every 3–5 minutes, maximum 3 mg; pacing or an epinephrine infusion if it fails. Tell the hospital about the metoprolol.

critical.scenario: A 68-year-old with a previous MI has palpitations for 45 minutes. Alert, BP 108/72. Regular wide QRS at about 170/min, no P waves visible.
critical.question: Rhythm and ALS treatment to anticipate?

options.t: Stable monomorphic VT: amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes or synchronized cardioversion per protocol
options.f: Correct. With heart disease, wide and regular is VT.

options.t: SVT with aberrancy: vagal manoeuvres only
options.f: Assume VT with known heart disease.
She has a pulse and a stable BP.

critical.explanation: It can degenerate to VF: pads on, close monitoring, and cardioversion if she becomes unstable.

critical.scenario: Bystander CPR is under way and the AED said "no shock". Your monitor shows narrow complexes at about 70/min. There's no carotid or femoral pulse. She had sudden chest pain and breathlessness before collapsing.
critical.question: Rhythm and likely cause?

options.t: PEA, likely from a massive pulmonary embolism: continue CPR, epinephrine, treat the cause
options.f: Correct. No pulse means PEA, whatever the monitor looks like.
Without a pulse it is PEA.

options.t: VF: the AED was wrong, shock now

critical.explanation: Epinephrine 1 mg every 3–5 minutes; pulmonary embolism may need thrombolysis on medical direction.
